chapters.name: Chapter 1: Getting ready to work with brands

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How athlete influencer deals work
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain what an NIL deal is and what is allowed for college athletes.
This lesson builds toward: Given your level of sport, you will explain what an NIL deal is and which rules apply to you, including what is not allowed, naming who to ask at your school or state and that NIL income is generally taxable.
An NIL deal pays you, in money, products or services, for letting a business use your name, image or likeness: social posts, appearances, camps, autographs or commercials.
For NCAA college athletes, the NCAA's NIL page says deals should pay you for the use of your NIL, have a real business purpose, and pay within a reasonable range. Pay-for-play, meaning pay to attend or play for a school or pay tied to your performance, is not allowed. At the time of writing, Division I athletes must report third-party deals of $600 or more through NIL Go, run by the College Sports Commission; ask your compliance office for current details.
High school NIL rules are set by each state's high school athletic association and state law; some states allow it with limits. Check yours before any deal. NIL income is generally taxable, so keep records and talk with a tax professional.
Step by step:
- Find your level: high school, NCAA division, NAIA, junior college or pro.
- Read your school's NIL policy or your state association's rules.
- Talk with your compliance office or athletic director.
- Keep a record of every deal and payment.
Words to know:
- NIL: name, image and likeness: earning from your name, photo or personal brand.
- Pay-for-play: pay to attend or compete for a school, or pay tied to athletic performance; not allowed under NCAA rules.
- Compliance office: the school office that explains and checks athletic rules.
Official sources:
- NCAA: Name, Image and Likeness
- College Sports Commission: Student-Athlete NIL Deals
- IRS: Self-Employed Individuals Tax Center
Try it now: Find your school's or state association's NIL page and write down three rules that apply to you and who you would ask with questions.
You can now explain how athlete NIL deals work and find the rules that apply to you.

check.q: What can an NIL deal pay you in?
check.why: NIL deals can pay in money, products or services for using your name, image or likeness.

check.q: You get your first NIL payment. What do you do?
options: Keep a record of it and talk with a tax professional
check.why: NIL income is generally taxable, so keep records and get tax advice.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Finding brands that fit you
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a list of five brands that match your values and audience.
This lesson builds toward: Given the products and local businesses you use, you will list five brands that fit your values and audience, with every restricted category for your school or state crossed out.
The best deals are with brands you already use and believe in, that your audience cares about. A local gym, a sports drink you actually drink, a training app you use, or a family restaurant near your school.
Start local. Local businesses are often more open to young athletes, and your local audience matters to them. Bigger brands often work through agencies or NIL marketplaces your school may use; ask your compliance office which ones are approved.
Avoid brands that clash with your values, your school's rules or your age, and many schools and states restrict categories like alcohol, tobacco, vaping, gambling and adult products.
Step by step:
- List products and local businesses you really use.
- Mark the ones your audience cares about.
- Cross out any category your school or state restricts.
- Keep your top five.
Words to know:
- Brand fit: how well a brand matches your values, image and audience.
- NIL marketplace: a website or app that connects athletes with brands for deals.
Try it now: Write a list of ten products or businesses you use. Ask an AI assistant which ones best fit an audience like yours, then pick your top five yourself.
You can now choose brands that fit your values, audience and rules.

options: They are often open to young athletes and care about your local audience
check.why: Local businesses are often more open to young athletes and value a local audience.

check.q: A vape shop offers you a deal. What do you do?
options: Accept if the pay is good
Cross it off; many schools and states restrict that category
Post about it without a deal
check.why: Avoid categories your school or state restricts, such as vaping.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Building your media kit
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Make a one-page media kit that shows brands your value.
This lesson builds toward: Using your app insights and a Canva template, you will create a one-page media kit with your bio, channels, real numbers, audience, offers and a safe contact, with every number real, current and dated.
A media kit is a one-page summary brands use to decide if you are a fit. It shows who you are, who your audience is, and what you can do for them.
Include: a good photo and short bio; your sport, team and achievements; your channels with follower counts and average engagement (likes, comments, shares or views per post) from your app's insights; who your audience is (location, age range if the app shows it); past partnerships; what you offer (posts, videos, appearances, camps); and contact info, using a sports email or a parent or agent for minors.
Use a Canva template to design it and an AI assistant to tighten the wording. Every number must be real and current. Do not buy followers; brands check engagement.
Step by step:
- Collect your real numbers from your app insights.
- Write a two-sentence bio.
- List what you offer.
- Design it in a Canva media kit template.
- Check every number; date it.
Words to know:
- Media kit: a one-page summary of who you are, your audience and what you offer brands.
- Engagement rate: how much people interact with your posts compared to how many follow or see them.
Try it now: Build your one-page media kit in Canva using your real numbers. Ask an AI assistant to make your bio shorter and clearer.
You can now build an honest one-page media kit.

check.q: What does engagement show in your media kit?
options: How much people interact with your posts
check.why: Engagement is likes, comments, shares or views per post.

check.q: Your follower count changed since you made your media kit last month. What do you do?
options: Update it with the real current number and date
check.why: Every number must be real and current.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Pitching a brand
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short, professional pitch message to one brand.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI draft, you will write a pitch message to one brand's official contact, under 150 words, in your voice, with a specific true reason, one idea and your media kit, and a parent involved if you are under 18.
A pitch is a short message asking to work together. Send it from your professional email or the brand's official contact, not random DMs to employees.
A good pitch: who you are in one line; why you love this brand (something specific and true); your audience and one number; one clear idea ("three training videos using your recovery app"); and your media kit attached. Keep it under 150 words.
Ask an AI assistant to draft it, then rewrite it in your voice. If you are under 18, have a parent or guardian involved. Follow up once after a week or two. Many brands will say no or not answer; that is normal.
Step by step:
- Find the brand's official contact.
- Ask AI for a short pitch under 150 words.
- Add a specific, true reason you love the brand.
- Attach your media kit.
- Follow up once after one to two weeks.
Words to know:
- Pitch: a short message proposing to work together.
- Follow-up: one polite reminder if you have not heard back.
Try it now: Pick one of your five brands. Use AI to draft a pitch, rewrite it in your voice, and have a coach or parent read it before you send.
You can now write and send a short, professional brand pitch.

check.q: Where should you send a brand pitch?
check.why: Send it from your professional email to the brand's official contact.

check.q: A brand has not answered your pitch after two weeks. What do you do?
options: Follow up once, then move on if there is no answer
check.why: Follow up once; many brands will say no or not answer, and that is normal.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Reading a deal: red flags
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Spot red flags in a deal before you sign.
This lesson builds toward: Given a written deal, you will check it for red flags with a trusted adult before signing, checking work, pay, length and how to end it, and refusing to sign under pressure.
Before you agree to anything, get it in writing and read it with a trusted adult. For bigger deals, a lawyer, agent or your school's NIL support can help. Do not sign under pressure.
Red flags: they ask you to pay money first; they want your passwords or login codes; the deal lasts a very long time or says they own your name or image forever; you cannot post for other brands at all (exclusivity) without fair pay; pay is unclear or only "exposure"; they want you to post things that are not true; or anything your school's or state's rules do not allow, such as using school logos without permission.
Check what you must do (how many posts, when, what), how and when you are paid, how long it lasts, and how to end it. College athletes: check if it must be reported and do that on time.
Step by step:
- Get the deal in writing.
- Read it with a trusted adult or adviser.
- Check work, pay, length and how to end it.
- Look for the red flags.
- Check your school and state rules and any reporting.
- Never sign under pressure.
Words to know:
- Contract: a written agreement both sides must follow.
- Exclusivity: a rule that you cannot work with competing brands.
- Usage rights: how and for how long a brand can use your photos, videos and name.
Official sources:
- NCAA: Name, Image and Likeness
- College Sports Commission: Student-Athlete NIL Deals
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to write a short sample NIL deal with three hidden red flags (it's practice). Find them, then write your own red-flag checklist.
You can now spot red flags in a deal and know who to read it with before signing.

check.q: Which is a red flag in a deal?
options: They want your passwords or login codes
A way to end the deal
check.why: Never give a brand your passwords or login codes.

check.q: A brand says you must sign today or lose the deal. What do you do?
options: Ask a friend to sign for you
Do not sign under pressure; read it with a trusted adult first
check.why: Never sign under pressure; get it in writing and read it with an adult.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Disclosing sponsored posts the right way
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a sponsored post with a clear, correct disclosure.
This lesson builds toward: For any post where a brand gave you something, you will write a sponsored post with a clear disclosure near the start, said and shown in video, not hidden in hashtags or your bio, and with no claim you cannot prove.
The FTC, the US agency that enforces advertising law, says you must disclose any material connection to a brand, which includes payment, free or discounted products, or a family or work tie, whenever you mention the brand.
Make it clear and hard to miss: put it with the post, near the start, using simple words like "Ad", "Sponsored" or "Thanks [brand] for the free shoes". In videos, say it and show it on screen; in live streams, repeat it. On photos and stories, put it on the image. Do not hide it in a pile of hashtags, only in your bio, or behind "more". Vague words like "sp", "collab" or "ambassador" alone are not clear.
Only say what is true: do not promote a product you have not tried, and never make health claims the brand cannot prove, like "this drink cures cramps".
Step by step:
- Decide: is there any payment, free product or tie? Then disclose.
- Put "Ad" or a clear thank-you near the start of the caption.
- In video: say it and show it.
- Use the app's paid-partnership label too, if it has one.
- Check that every claim is true.
Words to know:
- Material connection: a tie to a brand, like payment, free products or family, that people might not expect.
- Sponsored post: a post a brand paid for or gave you something for.
Official sources:
- FTC: Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers
- FTC: Endorsement Guides, What People Are Asking
Try it now: Final task: finish your media kit, brand pitch and red-flag checklist (with the names of who at your school or state you will ask). Then write a practice sponsored caption with a correct disclosure.
You can now post sponsored content with a clear, correct disclosure and stay within NIL rules.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Media kit Numbers missing, made up or out of date, or private contact details shown. One page with bio, channels, real dated numbers, audience, offers and a safe contact. Includes average engagement per post and a clear list of past partnerships or community work. Brand fit The chosen brand clashes with the athlete's values or a restricted category. One brand the athlete really uses that fits their audience and school and state rules. The choice is backed by a list of five fitting brands with reasons. Pitch message Long, generic or copied AI text, or sent to a random DM. Under 150 words, in the athlete's voice, with a true reason, one idea and the media kit, to an official contact. A parent or guardian is involved where needed and a follow-up date is set. Red-flag and rules checklist Missing key red flags or does not name who will be asked. Lists the red flags, what to check (work, pay, length, ending) and who at school or state to ask. Adds reporting deadlines and record-keeping for taxes. Disclosure No disclosure, or it is hidden or vague. A clear "Ad" or thank-you near the start, said and shown in video, with only true claims. Also uses the app's paid-partnership label and checks every claim with the brand. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which counts as a material connection you must disclose?
options: A free or discounted product from the brand
A brand you have never heard of
check.why: Payment, free or discounted products, or a family or work tie must be disclosed.

check.q: You are doing a sponsored live stream. How do you disclose?
options: Disclose clearly and repeat it during the stream
check.why: In live streams, repeat the disclosure.
